result:
The lamp was the only thing that mattered. Its brass fittings, polished with a soft cloth each morning, its great glass lens, a masterpiece of concentric prisms that could take a single, fragile flame and hurl it miles into the night. Elias was its keeper, a man for whom the world had shrunk to the twelve-foot diameter of the lantern room at the top of the tower.

His life was a rhythm of oil and wicks, of wind and salt spray. He knew the sea’s moods better than he knew his own. He could read a storm in the texture of the dawn and predict the height of a swell by the whistle of the wind through the tower’s iron lattice. For years, his only companions were the gulls that nested on the cliffs below and the silent, patient stars.

Sometimes, a ship would pass in the night, a cluster of lights against the void. For a fleeting moment, their paths would cross—his steady beam, their hopeful course—and then they were gone, leaving him to his solitary vigil. He was a fixed point in a world of motion, a promise of safety in the dark. He never felt lonely. How could he, when he held a star in his hands each night, a captive light meant for the lost?
